children: By Nate Raymond
A prominent Texas trial lawyer who played a leading role in litigation alleging Johnson & Johnson's
baby powder and other talc-based products caused cancer is joining a long-running, $10 billion shareholder lawsuit alleging the company concealed asbestos contamination in its talc products.
W. Mark Lanier on Monday

in the shareholder class action lawsuit in federal court in New Jersey. The case was filed in 2018, not long before Lanier won a judgment eventually worth more than $2 billion in favor of 22 women who blamed their ovarian cancer on asbestos in J&J's talc products.

The shareholder case is one of the key talc-related matters still confronting J&J after the company in June sought to resolve years of mass tort litigation through a roughly $5.5 billion settlement of thousands of cases by people saying they developed ovarian cancer after using its products.
Securities class actions rarely reach trial and often settle because of the potentially enormous damages at stake.

But lawyers at Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd, which serves as lead counsel for the plaintiffs, say they are preparing for trial after the US Supreme Court in April declined to review a ruling certifying the case as a class action.
"We have a dynamite team of trial lawyers," said Robbins Geller attorney Robert Henssler. "So we could certainly do it, but we're very excited to get to work with Mark Lanier."

Paul Geller, a founding partner at Robbins Geller who had worked with Lanier in prior litigation over opioids and the EpiPen allergy treatment, said his firm "wouldn't be bringing in Mark if we didn't think this case was likely to go to a jury."

Lanier, a partner at The Lanier Law Firm, is widely regarded as one of the nation's leading plaintiffs-side trial attorneys. He represented the plaintiff in a landmark trial in which a Los Angeles jury in March found Meta Platforms and Alphabet's Google liable for designing social media platforms that harmed young people.
He has a long history litigating against J&J, winning verdicts over metal-on-metal hip implants made by its DePuy unit before pursuing talc-related litigation.
"I am always pleased to work on cases with Robbins Geller pursuing a worthy cause," Lanier said in a statement.

Aviva Wein, J&J's worldwide vice president in charge of litigation, in a statement called the plaintiff's decision to seek to have Lanier join their legal team "perplexing," saying the company considers him a fact witness in the case.
"We intend to raise the appropriate objection with the Court," J&J said.
Lead plaintiff San Diego County Employees Retirement Association is pursuing the lawsuit on behalf of investors who owned J&J stock between February 22, 2013 and December 13, 2018.
The lawsuit alleges shareholders were harmed when J&J's stock price fell following developments that revealed information about asbestos in its talc products.
According to the lawsuit, those events included a Missouri jury awarding $4.69 billion in July 2018 to 22 women represented by Lanier, an award that was later reduced to $2.12 billion on appeal.
The complaint also cites a Reuters investigation published later that year reporting that J&J knew asbestos was present in its talc products, after which the company's stock fell 10%.
J&J denies wrongdoing and argues none of the events at issue disclosed new information correcting its prior statements about the safety of its talc products.
In asking the Supreme Court to hear the case last year, J&J
potential damages exceeded $10 billion. No trial date has been set.
The case is Hall v Johnson & Johnson, US District Court for the District of New Jersey, No. 18-01833.
For the plaintiffs: Darren Robbins, Tor Gronborg, Robert Henssler, Nathan Lindell and Hillary Stakem of Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd
For J&J: Kristen Seeger, John Skakun, Christopher Lee, Neil Conrad and Abigail Molitor of Sidley Austin
